name: create_artifact
description: Create an artifact: a titled, versioned item in this installation's shared catalog, visible to everyone who uses it. It is recorded as made by you, in the bot, task, project, or workspace you are working in. The call gives you its ID. For markdown or html, pass content to publish the complete entry (index.md or index.html) in this call. Prefer this when you already have the text; supply supporting text files inline, such as files: [{ "path": "style.css", "content": "body { color: inherit; }" }], so the entry and all assets appear together in version 1.0. Mix inline files with local copies as needed. Each file supplies either content with a required path, or fromPath with an optional path, never both. Every destination path must be unique; do not also supply the entry in files when using top-level content. Without content or an entry in files, it starts with a short entry holding its title. Make later changes with write_artifact_file and edit_artifact_file. An image, image series, video, or document needs its file from the start: pass it in files, such as { "fromPath": "out/chart.png" }. A copy keeps its own name unless you give it a path, so to publish a document you already wrote, copy it in as the entry: { "fromPath": "notes/plan.md", "path": "index.md" }. Write an artifact's files with write_artifact_file, which writes a whole text file, and edit_artifact_file, which replaces exact text in one, exactly as you would write and edit any other file: patch what changes instead of rewriting the whole page. Read them with read_artifact_file. These tools work directly on this installation's artifact catalog, so there is no copy on your machine: the shell cannot reach an artifact's files. To publish files you built with the shell or a script, or binary files such as images, pass them as fromPath files to create_artifact or update_artifact. Each call that writes an artifact makes its next version. You may change artifacts you created; changing one someone else made publishes a version everyone sees and needs the user's permission. A markdown artifact opens "index.md" and an html artifact opens "index.html"; put the pictures, styles, scripts, and other files they use beside them and refer to them with relative paths, such as ![Chart](images/chart.png) or , which resolve without rewriting. A file's media type comes from its path's extension. An html page runs as it is, scripts included, in a sandbox that cannot reach this installation's data. If a call would leave the artifact invalid, such as without its entry or over a size limit, it fails, no version is made, and you are told why. An open html page is drawn right in the reply at its full height, measured at the chat's width; inline, the page is never capped and never scrolls as a whole. "side" suits a page that needs its own scrolling, a full window, or long reading. An inline page is part of the reply, so write it as that part of the reply would read: laid on the chat itself, with no frame, no background, no outer card or panel, and nothing nested inside a box. Its first render decides its height, and the reply around it shifts whenever that changes, so design every state to fit it: size tabs to the tallest panel by stacking the panels in one grid cell, show details in a popover rather than an accordion that pushes content down, keep a long or changing list or log in one scrolling region of fixed height, and reserve room for data still loading, images (width and height, or aspect-ratio), and empty and error states. Never reach that height with padding: no large fixed or minimum heights that leave blank space, and nothing sized to the viewport, such as 100vh, because the frame grows to fit the page. If one state needs far less room than another, such as a short tab beside a long one, redesign so they match, by giving it useful content or showing both together; if you cannot, let the page shrink rather than leave an empty gap. Never use the default chatbot look: a stack of rounded cards, tinted callout boxes, or a highlighted coloured stripe down the left edge. Prefer clean visualizations, code examples and quotes, and file trees, and give hierarchy with spacing, hairline dividers, and type. DESIGN.md beside the Happy Agent documentation README is the full design system. Load Happy's standard styles first, with : with nothing else, the page looks like part of the app, in its fonts, colours, scrollbars, and inset, in light and dark, so leave html and body without a background, margin, or padding: the page is inset like the app's content beside the chat or on its own, and not at all inline, where it lines up with the reply. Beside the chat and on its own, Happy Desktop also centres the page in Happy's 912px content column, so never centre or cap it yourself with max-width and margin: auto on body; narrower content is fine. A dashboard, wide table, canvas, or other full-width app opts out with in , and only such a page may use width: 100vw. A game, canvas, drawing pad, or other single-screen app that page scrolling would fight, but never a document or dashboard meant to be read, opts into app mode with in : the host opens it full screen from a card, edge to edge with no scrolling or zoom, and owns its close control, a "×" in the top-start corner whose 48px the inset on that edge already holds; fill the viewport with height: 100%, handle resize and rotation, keep controls clear of env(safe-area-inset-*) and --happy-app-inset-*, and take touch, mouse, and keyboard. If the game needs that corner, move the "×" with (or bottom-start or bottom-end); an exit the page draws, such as Quit in a pause menu, calls window.happyApp.close(), and content="none", which hides the "×", is only for a page whose own exit is always clearly visible. Your own CSS always wins, so override only on purpose. Use its variables rather than fixed colours: --happy-text, --happy-muted, --happy-faint, --happy-border, --happy-surface, --happy-accent, --happy-added, --happy-removed, and --happy-chart-1 to --happy-chart-6, with --happy-font and --happy-mono for type. Load last for the standard components: shows a unified diff such as git diff writes (path="…" for one file, lines="40-52" for one range of it), and shows code, from a file of the artifact or a gives it a key-value store shared by all its versions and everyone using it, with realtime changes, writes that survive network failures, and who the viewer is. Before building one, read recipe/artifact-apps.md beside the Happy Agent documentation README. Call the API only at absolute /api/... paths, and put no files under api/. Read and change the data of an app yourself with read_artifact_data and write_artifact_data. Build and try the app in a folder of its own with happy-agent artifact dev as a workspace service, as two people and with network faults, then publish its files with fromPath in one update_artifact call, so people only ever see a finished version; after publishing, read_artifact_logs shows the errors and sync problems its pages reported. Types: "markdown" and "html" (the entry plus up to 255 other files; entry up to 4 MiB and 16 MiB), "image" (one PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, or SVG up to 32 MiB), "image_series" (1–64 images shown in path order, so number them like 01-intro.png), "video" (one MP4, WebM, QuickTime, or Ogg up to 256 MiB), "document" (one PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument, RTF, text, CSV, or EPUB file up to 64 MiB), and "gen_ui" (a Gen UI document, "index.genui.json" up to 256 KiB, plus up to 255 other files such as the images it shows). A version holds at most 256 MiB in all. A "gen_ui" artifact is a Gen UI document: native components such as stats, charts, tables, lists, steps, galleries, choices, and buttons that Happy clients draw with their own widgets. Use it when structure helps the reader, such as numbers to compare, options to pick from, things with a status, or a chart; keep explanations in prose. Pass the document as content; it becomes "index.genui.json". Nodes nest, with each node's props beside its type: { "genui": 1, "fallback": "the same in one or two plain sentences", "root": { "type": "card", "title": "Q3", "children": [{ "type": "stat", "label": "Revenue", "value": "$1.24M" }], "actions": [{ "type": "button", "label": "Break down by plan", "action": { "type": "message", "text": "Break down Q3 revenue by plan" } }] } }. Only containers take children, only a card takes actions, and an optional id names a node. A document that does not validate fails the call with each reason and the node it is about, such as "root.children[0].value"; fix them and call again. Pictures it shows must be files of the artifact, added with files and referred to by relative path such as "assets/photo.jpg"; remote image URLs are refused. Read genui/USAGE.md beside the Happy Agent documentation README before writing one, and genui/components/.md for each component's props. A good artifact has a cover and a summary. The summary is a short post under the title: what this is and the key takeaway, in a few sentences of plain text, line breaks fine, no Markdown. The cover is a WebP, either 16:9 (1600×900) or square (1200×1200), showing the headline, key number, or main chart, readable at feed size; the Feed shows it full width and draws nothing over it. Add one to any report, analysis, or result people would want to see in the Feed; scratch and utility artifacts may go without. For a chart or diagram, render it first with what you have, such as a headless browser screenshot, rsvg-convert, or matplotlib, and save it as WebP. A short looping animated WebP is fine; keep it small, and convert a GIF to one first: ffmpeg -i in.gif -c:v libwebp -loop 0 -q:v 75 cover.webp. PNG and JPEG are accepted; GIF is accepted but discouraged; SVG is refused. For example: files: [{ "fromPath": "out/cover.webp", "path": "cover.webp" }], cover: "cover.webp", summary: "Q3 revenue grew 18%, driven by enterprise seats.\nSelf-serve was flat, and churn fell to 2.1%." Change its title, background, display, cover, or summary later with update_artifact. For a running web page, use { type: "html", title, url, display? } without content or files. The URL is the content, never downloaded by the daemon. The client opens it through your network in a browser profile isolated to this artifact; cookies and storage are never shared with the workspace browser or other artifacts. Change the URL with update_artifact; its original network stays fixed and its fallback files cannot be edited. A live page holds no files, so it cannot have a cover; give it a summary.

display.description: How the chat first shows the artifact: "inline_expanded" starts open in the conversation, and "inline_compact" and "side" start collapsed to its title, which the reader can expand. Left out, html, gen_ui, image, image_series, and video artifacts start open and markdown starts collapsed.

background.description: Usually leave this out: the artifact then sits on the viewer's own surface and follows light and dark. Set a hex colour such as "#ffffff" only when the content needs one fixed canvas, such as a print-like document or a chart drawn for one palette. Must satisfy the required format.

cover.description: The path of the artifact's cover image among its files, such as "cover.webp": a WebP, still or animated, showing the headline, key number, or main chart, readable at feed size. A cover is either 16:9 (1600×900) or square (1200×1200); other shapes are refused. PNG and JPEG work too; convert a GIF to animated WebP first, and SVG is refused. An image artifact's cover is its own picture and an image series' its first, unless you name another or pass null.

summary.description: A short post shown under the title, like a tweet: what this is and the key takeaway, in a few sentences of plain text. Line breaks are fine; no Markdown. At most 5,000 characters.

content.description: The complete initial UTF-8 text of index.md (Markdown), index.html (HTML), or index.genui.json (Gen UI), published in version 1.0. May accompany auxiliary files, but not an entry in files or a live URL.

files.description: Files to publish together in version 1.0. Each item supplies either fromPath (a local copy, with optional destination path) or content (inline UTF-8 text, with required path), never both. Paths must be unique, including the entry supplied by top-level content.

fromPath.description: A file on your machine to copy in, such as an image you generated, a PDF, or a file you built with the shell

path.description: Where the copy sits in the artifact, such as "images/chart.png", or "index.md" to make it a markdown artifact's entry. Defaults to the file's own name. Must satisfy the required format.

content.description: The complete UTF-8 text of this artifact file.

url.description: A live http or https page instead of files; HTML only. localhost is your machine. Its network stays fixed for this artifact.
